15                               ANALYSIS                                  
16   A.   Motion by Cellars for New Trial.                                 
17        Cellars moves for a new trial and renews its motion for judgment as a matter of law 
18   (“JMOL”).  Cellars’ motions hinge on three main arguments:  (1) the affirmative defense of the 
19   Noerr-Pennington doctrine3 and litigation privilege under California law, (2) the Court’s judicial 
20   notice of documents, and (3) applicability of affirmative defense to the equitable claim for unjust 
21   enrichment.  As noted above, Cellars did not prevail on its claim for breach of fiduciary duty 
22   because the jury found that the gravamen of the claim for breach of fiduciary duty was based on 
23   the filing of Roach’s Texas litigation.  The Court DENIES these motions.  The law supports an 
24   instruction to the jury on the defense, and there was sufficient evidence on both sides to submit 
25   this issue to the jury for resolution.  The Court did not err in taking judicial notice of pleadings and

2        1.   Standard for Motion for Judgment as a Matter of Law.        
3        A motion for judgment as a matter of law (“JMOL”) is appropriate where “a reasonable 
4   jury would not have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for the [nonmoving] party on that 
5   issue.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50(a)(1).  A court can grant a JMOL “if the evidence, 
6   construed in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, permits only one reasonable 
7   conclusion, and that conclusion is contrary to the jury’s verdict.”  Pavao v. Pagay, 307 F.3d 915 
8   918 (9th Cir. 2002).  A court must uphold a jury’s verdict “it is supported by substantial evidence 
9   that is adequate to support the jury’s findings, even if contrary findings are also possible.”  
10   Escriba v. Foster Poultry Farms, Inc., 743 F. 3d 1236, 1242 (9th Cir. 2014).  A court must review 
11   the evidence as a whole and “disregard evidence favorable to the moving party that the jury is not 
12   required to believe,” and the court “may not substitute its view of the evidence for that of the 
13   jury.”  Johnson v. Paradise Valley Unified Sch. Dist., 251 F.3d 1222, 1227 (9th Cir. 2001) 
14   (internal quotations omitted).                                        
15        2.   Standard for Motion for New Trial.                          
16        For a motion for new trial, the Ninth Circuit has explained, “even if substantial evidence 
17   supports the jury’s verdict, a trial court may grant a new trial if ‘the verdict is contrary to the clear 
18   weight of the evidence, or is based upon evidence which is false, or to prevent, in the sound 
19   discretion of the trial court, a miscarriage of justice.’”  Silver Sage Partners, Ltd. v. City of Desert 
20   Hot Springs, 251 F.3d 814, 819 (9th Cir. 2001) (citing 4.0 Acres of Land, 175 F.3d 1133, 1139 
21   (9th Cir. 1999)).                                                     
22        3.   Affirmative Defense of Noerr-Pennington Doctrine and Litigation Privilege 
              Under California Law.                                       
23                                                                         
         Cellars argues that there were several errors all related to the affirmative defense of the 
24                                                                         
    Noerr-Pennington doctrine and litigation privilege under California law.  “The Noerr-Pennington 
25                                                                         
    doctrine derives from the First Amendment’s guarantee of ‘the right of the people . . . to petition 
26                                                                         
    the Government for a redress of grievances.’”  Sosa v. DIRECTV, Inc., 437 F.3d 923, 929 (9th Cir. 
27                                                                         
    2006) (quoting U.S. Const. amend. I).  The Noerr-Pennington doctrine provides that litigants who 
1   “petition the government for redress are generally immune from statutory liability for their 
2   petitioning conduct.”  Sosa, 437 F.3d at 929 (citations omitted).  There is an exception to the 
3   Noerr-Pennington doctrine, the “sham” litigation exception, Sosa, 437 F.3d at 932, which arises 
4   when the Noerr-Pennington defense is applied to antitrust claims.  The Noerr-Pennington doctrine 
5   applies to the filing of a petition and also to “conduct incidental to the prosecution of the suit.”  
6   Columbia Pictures Indus., Inc. v. Prof’l Real Estate Inv’rs, Inc., 944 F.2d 1525, 1528 (9th Cir. 
7   1991), aff’d, 508 U.S. 49 (1993); Freeman v. Lasky, Haas & Cohler, 410 F.3d 1180, 1184 (9th 
8   Cir. 2005).  The Noerr-Pennington doctrine applies to state law tort claims.  Theme Promotions, 
9   Inc. v. News Am. Mktg. FSI, 546 F.3d 991, 1007 (9th Cir. 2008).  In contrast to the California 
10   litigation privilege, the Noerr-Pennington doctrine does not provide immunity from suit but is an 
11   affirmative defense to liability.  Nunag-Tanedo v. E. Baton Rouge Par. Sch. Bd., 711 F.3d 1136, 
12   1140 (9th Cir. 2013).                                                 
13        The litigation privilege under California law is similar but not identical to the Noerr-
14   Pennington doctrine.  A “publication or broadcast” made as part of the “judicial proceeding” is 
15   privileged.  Cal. Civ. Code § 47(b).  The litigation privilege applies to all cases except claims for 
16   malicious prosecution, Silberg v. Anderson, 50 Cal. 3d 205, 213 (1990), as modified (Mar. 12, 
17   1990) (internal citation omitted), and claims for attorney malpractice.  Mindy’s Cosmetics, Inc. v. 
18   Dakar, 611 F.3d 590, 600 (9th Cir. 2010).  The litigation privilege is given a “broad 
19   interpretation” and “is not limited to statements made during a trial or other proceedings, but may 
20   extend to steps taken prior thereto, or afterwards.”  Action Apartment Assn. Inc. v. City of Santa 
21   Monica, 41 Cal. 4th 1232, 1241 (2007) (internal quotation and citation omitted).  The litigation 
22   privilege “applies to any publication required or permitted by law in the course of a judicial 
23   proceeding to achieve the objects of the litigation, even though the publication is made outside the 
24   courtroom and no function of the court or its officers is involved.”  Silberg, 50 Cal. 3d at 212.   
25             i.   Assertion of Affirmative Defense and Jury Instructions. 
26        Cellars argues that Roach first asserted this defense of the Noerr-Pennington doctrine and 
27   litigation privilege a month before trial.  However, Roach clearly listed this defense in his Answer.

13        Roach proposed the following jury instruction:  “One who files a lawsuit in a court of law 
14   is immune from liability for having done so.”  (Dkt. No. 231.)  Cellars objected and argued that no 
15   instruction should be given at all but not provide any alternate jury instruction.  (Dkt. No. 241.)  
16   The Court gave the following instruction on both the litigation privilege and Noerr-Pennington 
17   doctrine as follows, under the title of “Privilege”:                  
18             A person who files a lawsuit is immune from liability simply for 
              filing the lawsuit.  However, a person is not immune from liability 
19                                                                         
              from other actions.  You must decide if the gravamen – or heart – of 
20             the claim that Cellars brings for breach of fiduciary duty against 
              Roach is based on his filing of the Texas lawsuit.          
21                                                                         
    (Dkt. No. 265.)  In the verdict form, the jury answered “yes” to the question:  “Do you find that 
22                                                                         
    the gravamen – or heart – of the claim that Cellars brings for breach of fiduciary duty against 
23                                                                         
    Roach is based on his filing of the Texas lawsuit?”  (Dkt. No. 261.)   
24                                                                         
              ii.  Applicability of Privilege Defense to Claim.           
25                                                                         
         Cellars argues that the application of the litigation privilege and Noerr-Pennington 
26                                                                         
    doctrine as a defense was improper under the circumstances because that defense is not applicable 
27                                                                         
    in a case in which a client sues a former lawyer for breach of fiduciary duty.  Although there is 
1   case law indicating that the litigation privilege under California law does not apply to malpractice 
2   actions against an attorney, there is no case law indicating that actions for breach of fiduciary duty 
3   are barred.  And here, the rationale for excluding the defense for malpractice actions does not 
4   apply.  In a malpractice action, the dispute – if based on actions the former attorney took in 
5   litigation – centers on the actions the former lawyer took in the judicial process itself on behalf of 
6   its client.  For that reason, applying the litigation privilege does not make sense.  Here, in contrast, 
7   the crux of this dispute was not Roach’s action in representing Cellars; instead, the crux of this 
8   claim for breach of fiduciary duty was Roach’s attempt to gain ownership of Cellars.  The jury 
9   found that the claim arose out of his attempts in the Texas litigation to gain ownership of Cellars. 
10        Furthermore, there is no case law indicating that the Noerr-Pennington doctrine exempts 
11   claims for breach of fiduciary duty in this context, and for the same reason that the exception for 
12   litigation privilege does not apply, any exception would not apply to the Noerr-Pennington 
13   doctrine.                                                             
14             iii.  Sufficiency of Evidence.                              
15        Next, Cellars argues that it was error to instruct the jury and error to include Question 
16   Number 4 on the verdict because there was no evidence that Cellars’ claim was based on Roach’s 
17   filing and maintenance of the Texas litigation.  Cellars’ theory of breach of fiduciary duty was that 
18   Roach breached when he violated Rule 3-300 by entering into a business relationship with a client 
19   without a writing and without advising the client fully of the deal.  Cellars claimed that it was only 
20   harmed when Roach asserted his ownership rights over Cellars and forced Cellars to bring this 
21   claim for breach of fiduciary duty and incur legal fees in doing so.   
22        Despite Cellars’ theory, there was evidence to support the finding by the jury that the 
23   underlying basis of the breach of fiduciary duty claim was Roach’s action in filing and prosecuting 
24   the Texas litigation.  Even Cellars’ own pleadings support a theory that Cellars’ claim for breach 
25   of fiduciary duty was based on Roach’s filing of the Texas litigation.  Cellars first described the 
26   Texas litigation and then alleged in the section labeled “Breach of Fiduciary Duty”:   
27                                                                         
              Despite having voluntarily accepted the trust and confidence of 
              violation of this relationship of trust and confidence, Roach abused

2             ownership, possessory, and/or pecuniary interest in Schrader 
              Cellars, LLC by without notifying Plaintiff of his intent to do so, 
3             giving Plaintiff the opportunity to seek the advice of independent 
              counsel, or obtaining Plaintiff’s written consent.          
4                                                                         
    (Trial Exhibit 617 (FAC) at ¶¶ 13, 97).)  The way in which Roach attempted to gain a pecuniary 
5                                                                         
    interest was by filing and prosecuting the Texas litigation.  Thus, it was appropriate to present 
6                                                                         
    competing versions of the facts to the jury.                          
7                                                                         
              iv.  Litigation Privilege as a Matter of Law.               
8                                                                         
         Cellars argues that the Court was required to decided litigation privilege as a matter of law. 
9                                                                         
    However, the Court was not required to decide the issue of litigation privilege under California 
10                                                                         
    law because the facts were in dispute.  Cellars claimed that it filed its claim for breach of fiduciary 
11                                                                         
    duty against Roach because of his public comments about being an owner of Cellars.  Those 
12                                                                         
    comments explain why Cellars filed a claim to “quiet title” in this action, but they are not directed 
13                                                                         
    specifically at the claim for breach of fiduciary duty.  That claim was based Roach’s attempt to 
14                                                                         
    gain ownership of Cellars, and the issue for the jury was whether the claim for breach of fiduciary 
15                                                                         
    duty was based on Roach’s actions in the Texas litigation or simply his public assertion, outside of 
16                                                                         
    the Texas litigation, that he had an ownership stake in Cellars.      
17                                                                         
              v.   Failure to Instruct on Sham Litigation Exception.      
18                                                                         
         Cellars argues that the Court erred in failing to give an instruction on the sole exception the 
19                                                                         
    Noerr-Pennington defense – sham litigation, but Cellars never asked for or proffered one.  Also, 
20                                                                         
    given that the sham litigation exception applies in the context of antitrust litigation, under a 
21                                                                         
    rationale that does not apply here, there was no reason to provide that instruction.   
22                                                                         
              vi.  Wording of Jury Instruction.                           
23                                                                         
         Cellars argues that the Court’s instruction was improper because it was based on 
24                                                                         
    California’s anti-SLAPP action.  Yet Cellars provided, and still provides, no alternative.  The jury 
25                                                                         
    instruction provided and question on the verdict form reflects the law as described above.   
26                                                                         
         4.   Court’s Taking of Judicial Notice.                          
27                                                                         
         Cellars claims that the Court erred in taking judicial notice of three trial exhibits, 601, 617, 
1   and 648.  Trial Exhibit 601 was the First Amended Petition that Roach filed in the Texas litigation.  
2   The Court found that Trial Exhibit 601 was admissible.  (Dkt. No. 238).  This exhibit, along with 
3   other pleadings in the Texas litigation, were discussed as part of the statute of limitations issue – 
4   as to when Cellars was placed on notice that Roach was claiming an ownership interest in Cellars.  
5   Cellars initially questioned Roach about it.  (Tr. at 282:11-283:25.)  Cellars actually asked to enter 
6   into evidence Trial Exhibit 77, a pleading from the Texas litigation, to prove its point, and the 
7   Court admitted it without objection.  (Id.)                           
8        Roach was then questioned by his own counsel about Trial Exhibits 601 and 648, about 
9   some of the same issues.  (Tr. at 337:24-338:20.)  Cellars objected to Roach’s testimony about 
10   what the court ruled in the Texas litigation, and the Court sustained the objection but took judicial 
11   notice of Trial Exhibit 648 – an order in the Texas litigation.       
12        The Court also took judicial notice of Trial Exhibit 617, the First Amended Complaint that 
13   Cellars filed in this action.                                         
14        The Court took judicial notice of all three exhibits but instructed the jury as follows:

25   litigation to show what the parties asserted in this action and in the Texas litigation and when

27        5.   Unjust Enrichment.                                          
1   due to the privilege defense does not apply to its breach of fiduciary duty to the extent it seeks 
2   equitable relief – disgorgement of the wine paid to Roach.  According to Cellars, the conduct upon 
3   which it seeks equitable relief occurred before the lawsuit, so it cannot be barred by the privilege 
4   defense.  However, Cellars brought only one claim for breach of fiduciary duty.  As the Court 
5   found in the Order on the parties’ motions for partial summary judgment and adjudication, and as 
6   Cellars itself argued in its trial brief, Roach’s breach of fiduciary duty occurred when he, as an 
7   attorney, entered, or purported to enter, into an agreement with his client to obtain an ownership 
8   interest in Cellars in violation of Rule 3-300.  (Dkt. Nos. 168, 201.)  That one breach caused 
9   damage and gave rise to Cellars’ request for disgorgement.  The fact that Cellars seeks different 
10   types of relief incurred at different times – damages in the form of attorneys’ fees and 
11   disgorgement of the wine paid to Roach – for the same breach of fiduciary duty does not render its 
12   request for disgorgement a separate claim.  The jury found that Cellars’ one claim for breach of 
13   fiduciary duty was barred by privilege.  (Dkt. No. 286.)  The jury’s finding applies to the entire 
14   claim, including Cellars’ request to disgorge the value of the wine Roach received under the 
15   unenforceable agreement.                                              
16        Alternatively, to the extent Cellars could maintain a separate claim for breach of fiduciary 
17   duty based solely on the taking of fees or obtaining benefits in the form of wine under the 
18   agreement made in breach of Roach’s fiduciary duty, any such separate claim would be barred by 
19   the statute of limitations.  It is undisputed that the legal representation ended in 2016, five years 
20   before the lawsuit was brought.  If Cellars could bring a breach of fiduciary duty claim separate 
21   from its claim for damages, then the jury’s finding on statute of limitations would not apply.  The 
22   jury’s finding was premised on Cellars incurring damages by paying attorney’s fees to resolve the
